why: Two rules in `.tick/runners.toml` are enforced by two implementations in two
languages: `[sandbox].image` and `[orchestration].max_parallel`. Go owns the
format (internal/herd/config/load.go); the control plane reads both keys
before any container exists to read anything, so it re-implements them
(cloud/factory/src/repo-config.ts).
Until this file they were kept in sync by a comment saying 'mirrored from
internal/herd/config/load.go' — the one contract in this epic without a
cross-implementation test, while every other Go/TS shape has one
(tracker-layout.json, worker-boot-contract.json). .tick/learnings.md's rule
is explicit about why a comment is not enough: both suites stay green while
each side is internally consistent, so a one-sided edit is invisible.
Drift here already fails LOUD rather than silent — the sandbox entrypoint
refuses the boot when the image `tk` reads disagrees with the one the control
plane says it booted, and `kji`'s claim-time check inside each worker is the
authoritative wave-width bound no dispatch-side miss can bypass. So this
fixture is not closing a hole; it moves the failure from a container at run
time to a test at edit time.
It pins the RULES. The behaviour of the two image readers over whole TOML
documents is pinned separately, and case by case, in sandbox-image-cases.json.
internal/herd/config/runners_config_parity_test.go asserts this file against
Go's validator; cloud/factory/test/repo-config.test.ts asserts it against the
Worker's reader.
The pattern string itself is pinned, not just its effect: it is copied
character for character between `imagePattern` in internal/herd/config and
`IMAGE_PATTERN` in cloud/factory/src/repo-config.ts, and Go's
Regexp.String() and JavaScript's RegExp.source render it identically.
Deliberately narrow — an image reference is a name, never a place to hide a
shell fragment.
`max_length` is the schema's bound (`maxImageLen` / `MAX_IMAGE_LENGTH`).
Both sides build a reference of exactly that many `boundary_char`s, which
must be ACCEPTED, and one character more, which must be refused: a bound
pinned only from the outside would not catch an off-by-one.
image.refusal_message: is not a well-formed image reference

why: The wave width a cloud run's container fan-out must not silently exceed
(tick b6e). One bound, `>= 1`, enforced by Go's validator and by the
control plane's reader — and the refusal text is shared too, because the
two answer the same question and a config author should not be able to tell
which one refused.
`refused_toml_values` are raw TOML value texts rather than JSON numbers:
the point of those cases is that a typed value the schema does not allow is
a refusal on both sides, never a coercion, and only the TOML text can carry
the difference between 3, 1.5 and "3".
